lessons.title: Why we repair bags and tarpaulins
lessons.html:
Why we repair bags and tarpaulins

At a silo or depot, bags hold grain for storage and transport. Tarpaulins (tarps, or bokseile) are big covers that keep rain, sun, birds and dust off grain on trucks, in bunkers or in stacks. New bags and tarps cost a lot of money. A small hole that is repaired early saves a lot.

What damage does

  • A hole in a bag lets grain leak out. Grain is lost and the floor gets dirty. Spilt grain brings rats and birds.
  • A hole in a tarp lets rain in. Wet grain gets hot, mouldy and spoils. A whole bunker of grain can be lost from one leaking tarp.
  • Torn tarps flap in the wind and tear more.

Checking for damage

  • Look at bags when they are empty. Hold them up to the light to see small holes.
  • Spread tarps out flat on a clean, dry floor. Walk around and look for holes, tears, worn spots and broken eyelets (the metal rings for ropes).
  • Check ropes and straps.
  • Mark the damage with chalk so you can find it again.

Sort the damage

DamageWhat to do
Small hole or tearRepair it
Broken eyeletReplace the eyelet
Very big tears, rotten materialTell your supervisor; it may be scrapped
Oil or chemical stainsDo not use for food grain; tell your supervisor

Bags and tarps that touch grain must be clean. Never use a bag that had fertiliser, chemicals or cement for grain.

lessons.title: How to repair bags and tarpaulins
lessons.html:
How to repair

Tools and materials

  • Bag needle and strong twine.
  • Sewing machine for bags, if you are trained to use it.
  • Patches of the same type of material.
  • Tarp repair glue or tape for plastic tarps, as your site uses.
  • Eyelet punch and new eyelets.
  • Scissors or a knife, chalk and a measuring tape.

Repairing a bag

  1. Turn the bag inside out if your site does it that way.
  2. Cut a patch bigger than the hole on all sides.
  3. Sew the patch over the hole with small, tight stitches all around.
  4. For a split seam, sew the seam closed again with a strong stitch.
  5. Check the repair by pulling it gently.

Repairing a tarpaulin

  1. Clean and dry the area around the hole.
  2. Cut a patch bigger than the hole on all sides, with round corners so it does not lift.
  3. Glue, tape or sew the patch as your site method says. Press it down well.
  4. Let glue dry for the time on the tin before folding the tarp.
  5. To replace an eyelet, put a patch on the corner first to make it strong, then punch in the new eyelet.

Safety

  • Cut away from your body.
  • Keep fingers away from the sewing machine needle. Switch it off before you clear a jam.
  • Use glue in fresh air. Keep it away from flames. Wash your hands after.
  • Tarps are heavy. Lift and fold them with a partner.

Storing

  • Fold tarps dry. A wet tarp goes mouldy.
  • Store bags and tarps off the floor, in a dry, rat-free store.
  • Label repaired items and count them for the records.

Key points

  • Repair small damage early to save money and grain.
  • Check bags against the light and spread tarps flat to find damage.
  • Patches must be bigger than the hole on all sides.
  • Never use chemical or fertiliser bags for grain.
  • Fold tarps dry and store everything off the floor.

quiz.question: What can happen if a tarp over grain has a hole?

options.text: Rain gets in and the grain can spoil
The grain gets heavier and earns more

quiz.question: How big should a patch be?

options.text: Exactly the size of the hole
Bigger than the hole on all sides
As big as the whole tarp

quiz.question: How can you find small holes in a bag?

options.text: Hold it up to the light

quiz.question: What should you do with a bag that held fertiliser?

options.text: Use it for grain after shaking it
Patch it and use it for grain
Folded dry, off the floor, in a rat-free store
On the floor near the grain
